sweep_summary: Two title-hit items for Uab Meto, neither of which gives a stress statement for the language. (1) Himmelmann 2018 (open access, Zenodo; already on file, re-read): an areal chapter on intonation whose data languages are Totoli, Waima'a and Papuan Malay; no mention of Meto/Dawan anywhere in the text; only the general §3.1 caution that reported penultimate 'stress' in the region may be phrase-level edge tones — silent on the catalog coding. (2) Heston 2018 Diachronica (paywalled; abstract and landing page saved): diachrony of word prosody in Makalero and Fataluku (Papuan); not about Uab Meto; priority none. The catalog's fixed-strict penult coding (Steinhauer 1996a:224, stress on the lexical stem, usually its penult) stands; the best first-hand statement read in this sweep is Culhane 2018 p.9/p.58 (Amfo'an variety, on file from the prior audit), which confirms penult-of-the-foot stress with pre-foot syllables and enclitics outside the domain and refines rather than supersedes the deciding source; Edwards 2020 p.111 gives the same penult rule for Amarasi (a separate glottocode).

new_statements.quote: p.9: "All lexical roots in Amfo'an are comprised of a foot, which is minimally CV́V; word stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the foot. In Amfo'an, the prosodic word is minimally composed of a disyllabic foot ... extra material which is external to the foot, such as additional syllable or consonant, are dominated by the prosodic word. For example, maʔfénaʔ 'heavy' consists of one foot and one additional syllable." p.58: "enclitics are not prosodic words on their own, but are parsed with the host as one prosodic word. However, stress remains on the penultimate syllable of the host."
new_statements.citation: Culhane, Kirsten. 2018. Consonant insertions: A synchronic and diachronic account of Amfo'an. BA Honours thesis, Australian National University, 127 pp. hdl:1885/160794 (Amfo'an variety of Meto; Glottolog files it under uabm1237). NOTE: not one of the two sweep items — it was already on file from the 2026-09-16 audit and was re-read in this sweep; neither sweep item contains a first-hand Meto stress statement.
new_statements.locator: §1.5.2 'Syllable, foot and word', p.9; §3 p.58, ex. (117)
new_statements.reading: Fixed penultimate stress computed on the foot/lexical root, not on the whole word: pre-foot syllables (maʔ-fénaʔ) and enclitics (m-tóti=koo, n-béti=kau) are outside the stress domain, so surface words can carry stress on the antepenult or, with a monosyllabic-plus-prefix shape, on the final syllable. This agrees with Steinhauer 1996a:224 (stress on the lexical stem, usually its penult; petrified-prefix stems final) and with Edwards 2020 §3.3.4 p.111 for the sister variety Amarasi (amar1273; on file at 'Stress in Amarasi falls on the penultimate syllable of the prosodic word', with VVCV(C) words as the only exception). Confirms the catalog's fixed-strict penult coding with domain = stem/foot; refines it by making enclitic extrametricality explicit.

sources.quote: No language-specific statement on Meto/Dawanese; only the general caution (§3.1) that penultimate 'stress' reported for Austronesian languages of Indonesia and East Timor may be phrasal rather than lexical. Glottolog's tagging of this chapter to uabm1237 does not reflect Meto data in the text.
sources.locator: §3.1 (searched full text for Meto/Dawan/Amarasi: no hits)
sources.note: Areal chapter on intonation and information structure; its data languages are Totoli, Waima'a and Papuan Malay (Sources, p.372). A full-text search for Meto/Dawan/Atoni/Amarasi/Amfo'an returns no hit, so it contains no statement about Uab Meto. Its only bearing is the general caution (§3.1) that reported penultimate 'stress' in Austronesian languages of Indonesia and East Timor may be a phrase-final edge tone rather than lexical stress. Glottolog's tagging of this chapter to uabm1237 does not reflect Meto data in the text.
